content: Health insurance can cover either the full or partial costs of healthcare services, including wheelchair services. However, insurance plans often fail to achieve universal health coverage (UHC) because they tend to prioritize individuals with formal employment, excluding the poorest and most marginalized populations, such as women, who may not afford insurance premiums. Policy limitations, such as caps or restrictions on suppliers and products, can prevent wheelchair users from accessing suitable wheelchairs. In many cases, the establishment of wheelchair services relies on funding from national and international donors. However, donor funding is typically short-term and should be supplemented with advocacy for sustainable funding sources, such as government support. A funding model that prioritizes user choice and accommodates individual needs can empower wheelchair users to have a greater say in the purchasing process. Funding for wheelchair provision can be distributed through various mechanisms, such as health insurance purchase programs, voucher systems that allow users to make their own purchasing decisions, or loans that spread the cost over time. This funding may be provided directly to users or through wheelchair services and can be fully covered, cost-shared, or means-tested. To improve wheelchair provision, the sector must focus on mapping and strengthening relevant policies, establishing minimum quality standards for manufacturers, and creating tailored service protocols for different user groups. Dissemination of these guidelines will be facilitated by the World Health Organization (WHO) through webinars, conferences, and workshops, targeting a wide range of stakeholders, including health ministries, UN agencies, NGOs, professional associations, and organizations representing disabled and older individuals. The guidelines aim to guide member states in developing strategies to strengthen national wheelchair services, thereby improving access to high-quality, affordable services globally. This effort aligns with the goal of universal health coverage and the principle of leaving no one behind. Feedback mechanisms should be established to report product failures and improve wheelchair quality. Clear information about wheelchair products should be made available to users and service providers, and training for service personnel should include product-specific knowledge. Member states are encouraged to identify a minimum range of wheelchairs to be included in UHC and develop quality and safety standards for procurement. Sharing best practices and developing clinical guidelines tailored to user groups can enhance decision-making and efficiency. Early guidance on personnel roles and resource requirements is essential for developing national wheelchair provision systems. A competency framework for wheelchair service roles should inform workforce planning, training curricula, and accreditation processes. Engaging wheelchair user groups in decision-making and raising awareness about access to appropriate wheelchairs is crucial. Research gaps identified in the guidelines highlight the need for better data and evidence to inform policy and improve access to appropriate wheelchairs. Researchers and funding agencies are encouraged to address these gaps, focusing on outcomes critical to forming recommendations. Despite significant research growth since 2008, gaps remain in understanding the impact of service delivery steps, training, follow-up methods, and reporting outcomes. Further research is needed to evaluate the financial and economic aspects of wheelchair provision, including cost-effectiveness and equity. Monitoring and evaluation methods should focus on reducing harms and improving benefits for users and service providers. Developing a competency framework that bridges education and employment for wheelchair service roles will support workforce development and capacity building.
